title: How to Cook Chicken Breast Without Drying It Out
hook: Dry, rubbery chicken breast is the most common dinner disappointment. It's lean meat that overcooks in minutes. But with seven simple steps, you can cook chicken breast that is tender, juicy and safe, using just a pan, a little salt and a thermometer. It takes about thirty minutes, start to finish.
intro: Chicken breast has very little fat, so there isn't much margin for error. Two things cause most of the dryness. Uneven thickness, where the thin end overcooks while the thick end is still raw, and cooking it for too long. We'll fix both. We'll also use a quick salt brine for extra moisture, and a thermometer, which is the only reliable way to know when chicken is done. Let's get started. Even if you have never cooked chicken before, you can do this. It simply takes attention at the right moments.
youNeed: A meat mallet or rolling pin
youNeedNarration: Here's what you need. Two or three boneless chicken breasts. Coarse salt and pepper. A skillet with a lid. A little oil with a high smoke point. A meat mallet, or a rolling pin or heavy pan. And an instant-read meat thermometer. If you only buy one new kitchen tool this year, make it that thermometer. Nothing here is expensive, and most of it is already in your kitchen.
heroImagePrompt: Sliced juicy golden-brown chicken breast on a white plate with herbs, showing a moist interior, soft side light, shallow depth of field, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Even out the thickness
steps.narration: Step one. Place the chicken breast between two sheets of plastic wrap or baking paper on a cutting board. Using a mallet, a rolling pin or the bottom of a heavy pan, gently pound the thickest part until the whole breast is about three quarters of an inch, or two centimetres, thick. Don't pound it into a pancake, because you just want an even shape. Equal thickness means the whole piece cooks at the same speed, which is the key to juicy results. Very large breasts can also be cut in half horizontally to make two thinner cutlets, which cook faster.
steps.tip: Pound the thick end, not the whole breast
steps.mistake: Cooking a breast with one thick end
steps.imagePrompt: A chicken breast between sheets of baking paper being gently pounded with a rolling pin on a cutting board, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Brine it for moisture
steps.narration: Step two. Dissolve two tablespoons of salt in four cups, or one litre, of cold water. Put the chicken in the water, and leave it for thirty minutes in the fridge. The salt helps the meat hold on to more moisture while it cooks. If you're short of time, skip the brine, and instead salt the chicken generously on both sides fifteen minutes before cooking. Don't brine for more than an hour, or the texture can turn spongy. Raw chicken must always stay in the fridge. Always use a clean bowl and wash it afterward with hot soapy water, since raw chicken juices carry bacteria.
steps.mistake: Brining for hours and ending up salty
steps.imagePrompt: Raw chicken breasts resting in a glass bowl of salted water, kitchen counter, bright light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Dry and season well
steps.narration: Step three. Remove the chicken from the brine and pat it very dry with paper towels. Dry meat browns, wet meat steams. Don't rinse raw chicken under the tap, because that splashes bacteria around your sink. Brush each side with a teaspoon of oil, and season with pepper, paprika, garlic powder or any dry spices you like. If you skipped the brine, add salt now. Wash your hands and the board with hot soapy water afterward. Smoked paprika, garlic powder and dried thyme make an easy all-purpose rub, with no sugar to burn in the pan.
steps.mistake: Rinsing raw chicken in the sink
steps.imagePrompt: Hands sprinkling paprika and pepper on a raw chicken breast on a wooden board, close-up, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Sear in a hot pan
steps.narration: Step four. Heat a skillet over medium-high heat for two minutes, then add a thin layer of oil. When it shimmers, lay the chicken in the pan, presentation side down. It should sizzle right away. Leave it alone for five to six minutes without moving it, until the underside is a deep golden brown. Don't crowd the pan. If you're cooking more than two breasts, work in batches. That browned crust is where the flavor comes from. If the pan smokes heavily, lower the heat slightly. A deep golden color is what you want, not black.
steps.tip: Don't touch it for five minutes
steps.mistake: Moving the chicken before it browns
steps.imagePrompt: A golden chicken breast searing in a black skillet, light smoke, kitchen stove, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Flip, cover and lower the heat
steps.narration: Step five. Flip the chicken with tongs, then turn the heat down to medium-low and cover the pan with a lid. The trapped steam finishes the cooking gently, so the center cooks through without the outside burning. Cook for another five to seven minutes, depending on thickness. Don't keep lifting the lid, because the heat escapes. A gentle finish is the difference between juicy and dry chicken, so be patient and keep the heat low. If your breasts are very thin, three to four minutes will be enough, so start checking early.
steps.tip: Low heat plus a lid finishes it gently
steps.mistake: Leaving the heat on high to speed up
steps.imagePrompt: A skillet with a glass lid covering chicken breasts on a stove, steam condensation on the glass, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Check with a thermometer
steps.narration: Step six. Don't guess. Push an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the breast, without touching the pan. Chicken is safe to eat at 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or 74 Celsius. Take the chicken out of the pan once it reaches that temperature, because it keeps cooking a little as it rests. If it's below 165, cover the pan, and cook for a minute or two more, then check again. Cutting into it to look is not reliable, and it lets the juices escape. Check a second breast as well if you are cooking several, because they never finish at exactly the same time.
steps.mistake: Cutting the chicken open to check
steps.imagePrompt: A digital thermometer probe inserted into the thickest part of a cooked chicken breast in a pan, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Rest, then slice
steps.narration: Step seven. Move the chicken to a clean board or plate, and let it rest for five to ten minutes. The juices relax and spread back through the meat, instead of running out when you cut. Cover loosely with foil if your kitchen is cool. Then slice across the grain, in slices about half an inch thick. Serve in a salad, a sandwich or with vegetables. Store leftovers in the fridge within two hours, and eat within three to four days. Try the sliced chicken over a salad or inside a wrap for an easy lunch the next day.
steps.mistake: Slicing the moment it comes off the heat
steps.imagePrompt: A rested chicken breast being sliced on a wooden cutting board, juicy interior, photorealistic, no text

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Here are the mistakes to avoid. First, cooking a thick, uneven breast. The thin part dries out before the thick part is safe. Even it out first. Second, cooking without a thermometer. Overcooking by only a few minutes can ruin the texture, and undercooking is unsafe. And third, slicing right away. Resting keeps the juices where they belong. Do these three things right, and your chicken will be tender every time. Keep it simple, trust the thermometer, and enjoy the result.

recap.narration: Let's recap. Even out the thickness. Brine for moisture. Dry and season well. Sear in a hot pan. Flip, cover and lower the heat. Check with a thermometer for 165 degrees. And rest the chicken, then slice across the grain. Seven steps, about thirty minutes of cooking, and chicken breast that stays juicy. Even thickness, gentle heat and a short rest are the three secrets.
items: Flip, cover and lower the heat

outro: That's how you cook chicken breast without drying it out. If dinner was juicy tonight, subscribe to WikiTube, because we publish a new how-to every single day. Tell us in the comments how you season your chicken, and what you would like us to explain next. See you tomorrow. Next time, try different spices, because the method stays exactly the same.

metadata.title: How to Cook Chicken Breast Without Drying It Out
metadata.description:
Tired of dry, rubbery chicken breast? In this step-by-step video you'll learn how to cook chicken breast without drying it out: even out the thickness, brine for moisture, dry and season, sear in a hot pan, finish covered on low heat, check with a thermometer for the safe 165 degrees Fahrenheit (74 Celsius), then rest and slice. A simple stovetop method for juicy, tender chicken every time.

You'll need: boneless chicken breasts, salt and black pepper, a skillet with a lid, a meat thermometer, a meat mallet or rolling pin.

short.title: Juicy chicken breast in 3 steps #shorts
short.description: Even thickness, hot pan, thermometer. Full 7-step guide on the channel. #chicken #cooking #howto
short.hook: Stop drying out your chicken breast.

steps.title: Even it out
steps.narration: One. Pound the thick end until the breast is an even thickness, then dry and season it.

steps.title: Sear, then cover
steps.narration: Two. Sear in a hot pan for five minutes, flip, cover, and cook on low.

steps.title: 165 and rest
steps.narration: Three. Take it out at 165 degrees Fahrenheit, 74 Celsius, and rest it for five minutes.
